title: SceneSmith: Agentic Indoor Scene Generation
one_liner: A framework that uses language-model agents to build rich, physically accurate virtual rooms for robot training by assembling architectural layouts, furniture, and small objects in sequence.
lead: Robots trained in simulation need environments that look and behave like real homes. Today's simulators make sparse, unrealistic rooms. SceneSmith solves this by having three language-model agents work together: one designs the overall scene, one critiques what was built, and one coordinates the steps. The result is dense, physically stable virtual rooms that robots can actually learn from.

problem.h2: Sparse simulations fail to train real robots
paras: Simulation is how robot engineers train and test policies cheaply before deploying a robot into a real home. But today's simulators generate rooms with a few chairs and tables, no clutter, and no small objects to manipulate. A real kitchen has a fruit bowl, canned goods, dish racks, and loose fruit scattered around. A bedroom has books, shoes, a lamp, and folded clothes.

When a robot trained on a sparse simulation meets a real home, it freezes. The dense clutter was never in its training examples. Prior methods—simple procedural rules, data-driven placement, or basic language-model prompts—all treat small objects as an afterthought and skip the articulated details (drawers, cabinet doors, hinges) that a real robot must learn to manipulate. The result: a trained policy fails on real homes.

callout.html: Current simulators generate sparse, unrealistic rooms that lack the density and physical detail robots need to learn general manipulation.

steps.text: A language model reads the task description and generates diverse prompts describing a realistic room layout.
For each object or area, the router decides: generate a new 3D object from text, retrieve an existing articulated model from a library, or apply a thin texture wrapper.
Generated objects are checked for validity; articulated furniture is retrieved with collision meshes (the outlines that say where the object is) and joint definitions already built in.
Large rooms are placed first, then furniture into rooms, then small objects on surfaces, checking for collisions at each step.
A language model checks whether the final scene matches the task and looks realistic; if not, the designer adjusts and repeats.

paras: SceneSmith changes the asset composition strategy. Instead of treating objects as a single flat list placed all at once, it decomposes scene construction into a hierarchy: architectural layouts, then furniture, then small objects, each using a different acquisition method matched to the object type.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: Physical stability margin
hidden.name: Physical stability margin
paras: Every object placed in a simulator has a real physical center-of-mass, size, and weight. An object on a table is stable only if gravity and friction keep it from tipping, sliding, or falling through the surface. The paper measures this as a single score: the fraction of objects that remain still under physics simulation for a full episode (96% in their results). This is the litmus test for whether a scene is usable for robot training.

To achieve this, SceneSmith estimates mass and friction per object, computes the collision outlines (the mesh boundaries that define where each object occupies space) for articulated parts like drawer hinges and cabinet joints, and runs a placement algorithm that checks for overlaps before committing each object to the scene. Objects that would be unstable are either repositioned or rejected.

heat.caption: Darker means more physically stable; highlight shows objects that remain stable under physics simulation.

reads.html: An object is stable if it does not tip, slide, or sink under gravity and friction after the scene is created and physics runs.

The paper reports a stability rate as the percentage of generated objects that remain fixed-in-place or at-rest after a full physics simulation episode, measuring collision-mesh correctness and physical property estimation accuracy.

paras: A flat approach—asking a single model to place all objects at once—creates collisions and instabilities, because the model has no feedback loop and no way to reason about spatial constraints. SceneSmith succeeds because it breaks the problem into stages, each with a specific role: the designer works at a high level (task description to room sketches); the asset router reasons about object type and context (static, articulated, or textured); and the orchestrator places objects hierarchically (rooms first, then furniture in rooms, then small objects on surfaces), checking for collisions after each step.

The critic agent closes the loop: if the result is not realistic, the designer generates a new candidate. This iterative refinement is what prior flat methods lack. Additionally, by integrating physical property estimation (mass, friction, inertia) into the asset router, each object carries its own physics, so the placement algorithm does not have to guess. The hierarchical stages mean that later objects are constrained by earlier choices, making collisions rare and physics-correct.

stages.s: Task (e.g., pick fruit and place on plate)
Designer proposes room layout and object categories
Asset router decomposes each request and selects generation, retrieval, or texture wrapping
Orchestrator places hierarchically: rooms, then furniture, then small objects; checks collisions at each step
Critic agent verifies realism and prompt faithfulness; if fail, loop back to designer
Physics-ready scene with 3-6x more objects than prior methods

math.words: For each object placed, check collision geometry and estimate the restoring force (mass and friction). Penalize placement if restoring force is too small.
symbols: estimated mass of object i (in kg)
estimated friction coefficient of the supporting surface for object i
the downward pull on object i due to gravity and tilt
volume of overlapping geometry between object i and other objects (zero means no overlap)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Object 1 (apple): mass 0.1 kg, friction 0.6, no tilt, collision volume 0. Restoring force = 0.1 * 0.6 = 0.06 >> gravity component 0.01. Stable.
Object 2 (large book): mass 0.8 kg, friction 0.3, no tilt, collision volume 0. Restoring force = 0.8 * 0.3 = 0.24 >> gravity 0.02. Stable.
Object 3 (thin vase): mass 0.2 kg, friction 0.1, tilted 10 degrees, collision volume 0. Restoring force = 0.2 * 0.1 = 0.02, but gravity component with tilt ≈ 0.04. Unstable. Reject or reposition.

math.note: Objects with high mass and surface friction resist sliding; those with zero collision volume do not penetrate other objects. Both conditions must hold for stability.

charts.title: Prior methods (sparse)
charts.note: Old simulators place only large furniture and few small objects; articulated details and physics properties are absent.

charts.title: SceneSmith
charts.note: SceneSmith generates 3-6x more objects, includes articulated furniture with joint definitions, and validates stability under physics.

items.html: If the language model asks the text-to-3D system for a shape it cannot produce (e.g., self-intersecting meshes where the surface crosses itself), the asset router must fallback to retrieval or texture wrapping. If no fallback is available, the object is skipped, reducing scene density.

items.b: Articulated library does not have the requested object type.
items.html: The system retrieves articulated furniture from ArtVIP; if the requested object (e.g., a specific brand of refrigerator) is not in the library, the system retrieves a close semantic match, which may not fit the scene aesthetically or physically.

items.b: Mass and friction estimates are inaccurate.
items.html: The system estimates mass per link based on volume and material; if the estimate is wildly off (e.g., a plastic toy guessed to be ceramic), the stability check may pass when the object would tip in reality, or reject valid placements.

The language model may propose rooms with contradictory constraints (e.g., three windows on a 2-meter wall) that the orchestrator cannot satisfy; the critic catches obvious failures but may miss subtle ones.

items.b: Done right: hierarchical stages + critic loop.
items.html: When the designer proposes, the router routes intelligently, the orchestrator checks collisions hierarchically, and the critic refines iteratively, the system avoids these pitfalls and generates scenes that are dense, realistic, and stable.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a demo that takes a simple task description (e.g., 'a kitchen where a robot picks a fruit from a fruit bowl') and generates a scene. Then drop that scene into a robot simulator and run physics for 5 seconds. Count the number of objects and measure the fraction that remain in place (not tipped, slid, or sunk). Compare against a baseline that places objects randomly or in a single flat pass.
demo.metric_eq: Stability rate = (objects at rest after 5s physics) / (total objects placed). Target: > 90%.
demo.closing: The demo makes one thing impossible to miss: hierarchical, critiqued generation produces scenes where almost everything stays put, while flat methods have 30-50% of objects tip or disappear.
